utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mrs. Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis. We are assisted by our intern Ms. Jaspreet Saini, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the other Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rod Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, in particular, the members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in or around the courtroom. We will be hearing a witness, whose testimony will take a number of days. Without wasting any more time, could the usher call the witness into the courtroom, please. Defence, is there anything you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I would first like to make sure that you're receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say that you can hear me and you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first and last names, your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dzemal Merdan. I was born on the 6th of June, 1950 -- on the 6th of August, 1950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were born on the 6th of August, 1950. Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Busovaca, in the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you currently hold a position of any kind, and if so, what position do you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind, and if so, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that period of time I did not hold a position of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you didn't hold a position, did you have a civilian role or a military role of some kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I didn't understand the year you referred to. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was a slip of the tongue. In 1992, towards the end of 1992, and in 1993, I did hold a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In mid-1992, I was in the Territorial Defence, and in 1993, I was a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a member of the BH army, where were you assigned, and what rank did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, to be more precise, in December, when the BH army corps was formed, I was the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. And during that period of time, I did not hold a rank of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have testified before the Hague Tribunal already, and I have testified before the district court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the witness is to tell you where he testified, it might be preferable to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll go into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You now have to read out the solemn declaration. Could you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we give the floor to Defence counsel, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we'll be following here over a two-week period. Initially, the Defence, who are to your left and whom you have met, will conduct for a three-day period - Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday, since there won't be a hearing on Wednesday - the Defence will conduct its examination-in-chief, and this will take up three days. After they have completed their examination-in-chief, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will conduct what we call their cross-examination. As a rule, if the Defence takes three days, the Prosecution will also be granted three days to examine you. This means that the Prosecution will examine you on Friday, and Monday and Tuesday of the following week. After that stage, Defence counsel may re-examine you. Once Defence counsel has completed its re-examination, the Judges, who are sitting before you, will also put questions to you. According to the Rules of Procedure that govern this Tribunal, the Judges may ask a witness questions at any point in time. But as a rule, for the sake of efficiency, the Judges prefer to wait for the parties to complete their examination before they put questions to a witness. Usually the questions that the Judges put are put to the witness to clarify certain answers, or sometimes the Judges may feel that there are certain gaps in your answers and as a result the Judges will ask you questions in such cases, too. And when you reply to questions, you might be shown documents by the parties or by the Judges. You might be shown military documents and asked to comment on the documents. As you're already aware, since you already testified here, the procedure followed is an oral procedure, and your answers will provide the Judges will information about the events that took place in 1992 and 1993. The answers you give are transcribed so that there's a transcript of the questions and the answers. And this is why your answers are so important. If you fail to understand a question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. Sometimes the questions might be very complicated, and if that's the case, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it, because it's necessary for your answers to be precise. In addition, I would like to point out two other important Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. factors, in particular given the position you held in the past. You have taken the solemn declaration; you said you will speak the truth, and this means you should not give false testimony. False testimony is an offence that can be punished by this Tribunal. A witness could be given a fine or a prison sentence, or both measures could be taken. It is your duty to testify, and as you have taken the solemn declaration, you are no longer a witness who belongs to either of the parties, you will be testifying in the interests of justice. Secondly, I would like to point out the following: When you answer a question, if you believe that the answer you provide could be used against you at some subsequent date, you may refuse to answer that question. The witnesses have these rights, because the witnesses should not be placed in a position where they might incriminate themselves. This is a measure that exists in the criminal code of a number of countries. But in such very rare cases, the Trial Chamber may, nevertheless, compel the witness to answer the question. However, the Chamber grants the witness a form of immunity. I wanted to point this out to you. This is how we will be proceeding here. The hearings might be quite tiring, because witnesses might be under stress, but we will be having breaks which will allow you to rest. And we also have to have these breaks for technical reasons. Every hour and a half we will have a break that will last between 20 and 25 minutes. So you will have two breaks every day that will allow you to have one hour's rest. When we have hearings in the afternoon, we work from 2.15 until 7.00 p.m.; in the mornings we start at 9.00 and finish at 1.45. But on Thursday and Friday, the hearings will be held in the morning, and next week the hearings will be held in the morning, too; however, on Tuesday and Wednesday, our hearings will be held in the afternoon. I wanted to provide you with this information to ensure that we can proceed smoothly. But rest assured the parties don't want to place you in a difficult condition. All they want is to make sure that you can contribute establishing the truth. If you encounter any difficulties or feel you need to have a rest, please inform us of the fact. We will try to grant your requests if we believe that they are justified. I will now give the floor to Defence counsel who will provide you with additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Merdan.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you've just been told by the Presiding Judge, I'm going to give you another piece of information. We both speak the same language, and you are in a position to answer my question immediately. However, my question and your answer are being interpreted into two languages for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom. That is why I would like to ask you to make a pause between my question and your answer. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Where do you currently reside, Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I currently reside in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that you're retired. Can you please tell me, what was your profession before you retired, while you worked?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Throughout my entire career I was a professional officer, a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about your education, where and when you completed it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in my native village, Busovaca. This lasted eight years. I went to the secondary school in Travnik for four years, and I graduated in 1969. After that I went to the naval academy. I stayed there for four years, and I graduated from the naval academy in 1973. I also completed the Command Staff College in 1975. This Command Staff College enabled me to acquire a theoretical knowledge that enabled me to perform very high duties in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve in the JNA, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Throughout my engagement in the former Yugoslavia, I served in the navy of the JNA, and all this time I spent at the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer of the JNA, did you have a rank? What rank was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. My last rank in the JNA was the frigate captain. This is a very specific rank in the navy. In the army, it would be lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you leave the JNA at any point in time? If that was the case, can you tell us why you did that.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I left the JNA or the navy in 1992 -- to be more specific, towards the end of 1992, after having noticed that there were some changes and processes in the JNA that I could not subscribe to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said towards the end of 1992. Is that a slip of the tongue, or ...

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise, Your Honours. I misspoke. This was in 1991, and it was obviously a slip of the tongue on my part, the second one today. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991, when you left the navy of the JNA, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I served on the island of Vis towards the end of my service, and this is where I left the navy. I spent some time in Split, and after that I went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA and the Serbian forces attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of April 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At the beginning of April 1993, I was in Busovaca, and from time to time I would go to Zenica to spend some time with my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told the Presiding Judge that you are retired. In the JNA you had a rank that was the equivalent of a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, could you please ask the witness, at the beginning of April 1993, was that the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, this would be the beginning of 1992. It seems that we are making quite a lot of mistakes when it comes to years today. Yes, it was the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were retired. Could you tell us whether in the BH army you acquired another rank, and what was the rank that you held when you were retired?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In the BH army I acquired two ranks, and when I was retired, I was a general.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, when the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you join any of the formations that existed at the time, and if that was the case, could you tell us what formation was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: When the war started in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I joined the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, at the time, as far as the legal provisions and other enactments were concerned, was the only armed force of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which unit or staff did you join in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In 1992, when the war broke out in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I joined the district staff of the Territorial Defence, covering the region of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in 1992, did you have a position? Did you perform any duties in the Territorial Defence staff? And if you had a duty, can you tell me what that duty was and until when?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In April 1992, when I joined the Territorial Defence, in other words the district staff of the words, the district staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica, I performed the duties of one of the assistants of the commander of this staff. Towards the end of May or beginning of June of 1992 - I can't recall the exact date - I was appointed commander of the regional staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina towards the end of October 1991. As an officer of the former JNA, you must have followed the developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell me, did you know at the time what was the attitude of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the preservation of the then-existing state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I followed the developments of the former Yugoslavia as much as I could. I followed the events that took place in 1992 -- in 1990 and 1991 and 1992. As far as I was informed at the time, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina strived to preserve the unity of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, but it also wanted to see all the republics of the former state to have quality. And they wanted all of the republics to remain as integral parts of that former state.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, we already know that in 1991, the war broke out first in Slovenia and then in Croatia. Do you know whether, toward the end of 1991, Bosnia-Herzegovina took any measures in order to proclaim its own sovereignty and independence?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. I followed those developments, and as far as I knew at the time, Bosnia-Herzegovina endeavoured and tried to preserve unity. However, since there was a war in the Republic of Croatia, and before that in the Republic of Slovenia, and one could already see that these developments would result in the breakup of Yugoslavia, Bosnia and Herzegovina did not want to remain as part of Yugoslavia without the republics of Croatia and Slovenia, because it was obvious that the republics of Croatia and Slovenia would secede.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Bosnia-Herzegovina and under what conditions and when was recognised as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Within the framework of the measures undertaken by Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bosnia-Herzegovina did request to become an independent and sovereign state, and I know that this was discussed at very high state and military levels outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that Bosnia-Herzegovina met almost all criteria to become an independent state. The only thing that was still missing was a referendum that was to show the will of the people and to demonstrate whether the people were for or against the independency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did this referendum take place? And when about Bosnia-Herzegovina become an independent state?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At that time I followed the events very closely, and I know that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did organise a referendum and that this referendum was very successful, and that Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its independence on the 6th of April, 1992. This independence was recognised by the countries of the European Union, the Republic of Croatia, and somewhat later the United States of America. And after that, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by a series of countries in Europe and all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer of the JNA, did you know what measures were put in place in 1991 and 1992 in order to weaken the defence power of various republics, and especially of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I know quite a lot about this problem. The Yugoslav People's Army Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at that time was one of the four leading armed forces in Europe. It tried to weaken the defence power of the Territorial Defence, and the Territorial Defence was under the authority of the respective republics. The Territorial Defence was weakened, and it was disarmed in the following way: The arms of the Territorial Defence was placed in the barracks under the control of the JNA or in the depots of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I'm going to be using documents in my next questions, I would kindly ask the usher to give the witness the binder, and my following set of questions will be divided into several parts: The first one will be the organisation of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the 3rd Corps; the second part will be the relationship with the HVO; the third part will be the information that the general has about the indictment; and the fourth part will be relative to his knowledge and information about the presence of foreigners in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The binder that I would kindly ask to be provided to the generals are relative to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution -- does the Prosecution have a right to the binder as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we could not buy enough binders over the weekend, and that is the only reason why we haven't provided them with a binder. I'm sure our learned friends will understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at the first four documents which you can find after tab 1. The numbers are 1643, 1644, 1697, and -- actually, the first three documents, that is, and then the penultimate one in this part, number 1663. The first document is by the command of the 1st Military District, and given what you have already told us, would you -- when looking at the first and third paragraphs of this document, would you be able to recognise the behaviour of the JNA on the eve of the war? In other words, its organisation and mobilisation for the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know if it's just the pile that we received or if it's the Chamber's as well, but we don't seem to have the translations of these documents. I know the Defence have addressed this issue in the past, but I do believe it's important for the record to reflect, when they are showing documents to the witness for which there's no translation, that that be put into the record. Alternatively, if there are English translations available, we'd be grateful if we could be provided with those.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must say that very few documents from the new list will be shown to the witness only in B/C/S, because it was not possible for these documents to be translated. And for them we're just going to be given numbers for identification. That's why I'm going to ask the witness to read the title and the date on the document, and this will enable us to later identify the documents not only by the Defence numbers but also by the title or the name of the documents themselves. This is what you have already suggested that we could do with regard to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said that if there were any translation problems, the witness would read out the paragraph that the Prosecution wanted the witness to identify. We will mark this document for identification and wait for the final translation to be provided, because the Translation Unit wasn't able to translate all the relevant documents in good time. Mr. Mundis -- so this will be the case for the first document, number 1643. There is no English translation of that document, but the witness could read out the paragraph concerned. I believe that that would be the third paragraph that is underlined. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I should also at this point just note that the four documents that the witness is being shown were not on the list that we were provided on the 29th of November, 2004, with respect to documents likely to be used with the witness. I am aware that the Defence disclosed to us just this morning a rather large number of new documents pursuant to their new exhibit list, but we were certainly not notified of any of those documents being likely to be shown to the witness today. And I simply put that on the record at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It appears, according to the Prosecution, that there are four documents which aren't included in the official list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these documents are on the official list of documents that we provided on the 3rd. This is the additional list of documents, and since we disclosed all these documents to the Prosecution today and a list of documents, it's correct to say that they were not included in the previous list, which is why we weren't able to inform the Prosecution of our intention to use them. But as far as these new documents are concerned, they represent only a small percentage of the total number of documents. I don't believe that they're more than 5 per cent of new documents in this new list. But since the Prosecution will only commence its Prosecution in four days' time, I believe they will have time to familiarise themselves with the documents that were disclosed to them this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please read out the third paragraph in this document so that everyone can hear what is at issue. And could you tell me whether this is one of the documents on the basis of which you're aware of the fact that the JNA was preparing for a war at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness could also tell us who drafted the document, because the Prosecution and the Judges would like to know where this document comes from. The witness could read out the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this document was issued by the command of the 1st Military District on the 7th of October, 1991. It was filed under number 115/123. The title of this document is "Report on the Meaning of the Declaration of an Imminent Threat of War in the Country," and it is forwarded to the command of the Sarajevo Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out the third paragraph, too, and could you answer my question of whether, as far as you know, at the time the JNA was preparing for the war that would break out.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: "The decision of the Presidency and the statement of the federal secretary for national defence are the basis for taking broad social action, including propaganda and carrying out tasks by commands of military districts, or rather, all military and territorial organs of the JNA. This should include sending mobilised men and volunteers to all units of the JNA. The organs of power and the commands of military districts shall coordinate all activities involving propaganda, mobilisation, and the organisation of receiving volunteers and sending them to the deployment areas of the JNA war units."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as a soldier, did you know that the army, when there was an imminent threat of war, called on -- people had wartime assignments in the JNA or did they gather volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: As a soldier, I know that the Yugoslav People's Army had to have a reserve force that it would use to bring units up to strength. And here I can see that they've mentioned taking in volunteers. Since this document is dated October 1991, I already observed in the Republic of Croatia, while I was in the service, that there were volunteers reporting to the JNA, and they didn't resemble the type of soldiers one was supposed to have in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at another two documents now. Could you read out who the document was drafted by and who it was forwarded to. And does this demonstrate the relation or the attitude to weakening the defence capacity of the Territorial Defence? The documents are 1644 and 1697.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The first document is from the republican staff of the Territorial Defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's dated the 18th October, 1991. It's addressed to the regional staff of Territorial Defence, to all regional staffs, to the town Territorial Defence staff in Sarajevo, and there's something I can't read here. This is a report on the men present in staffs and Territorial Defence units. It's an order. The second document is dated December 1991. Again, it's from the Territorial Defence republican staff, and it's addressed to the Federal Secretariat For National Defence, the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY. It's called "Organisational Changes in the Territorial Defence of the BH," according to a plan Jedinstvo 3, that's a report. Thank you for your warning. I will try to pay attention to it. These two documents show that the Territorial Defence strength is being reduced. It shows by what percentage the units of Territorial Defence have been weakened in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, so everyone can follow, on the last page of the first document, could you say what the situation was on the 31st of December, '85? And what was the numbers on the 31st of December, 1991? We can see that in the first column. And what was the extent of the reduction, which we can see in the last column?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, this table shows quite clearly that the reduction in the forces of the Territorial Defence was very significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read out the first figure, please, towards the end of 8085, and the last one at the end of 1991, or rather the percentage of reduction which we can see in the last column.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: On the 31st of December, '85, the number of men was 313.990.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 310.530. Are you looking at the table?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: You asked me about the strength.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. 313.990.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: On the 31st of December, 1991, the Territorial Defence had 86.164 staff members, and when we make the calculations and when we turn this into percentages, this represents a reduction of 82.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the third document, could you please read out -- you've already said who drafted the document and who it was forwarded to. Could you just read out the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: "On the basis of conclusions, the tasks, the guidelines received from the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, and on the basis of the analysis carried out regarding the organisational changes made and the changes to the units within the Territorial Defence of the BH, in accordance with the Jedinstvo plan, in 1991 a suggestion was drafted for a new organisational structure of the Territorial Defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and for reducing it to a number representing less than 2 per cent of the population within the republic."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, tell me, when the JNA and the Serbian forces attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina, what sort of condition were the BH armed forces in?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I've already said that at the beginning of the war, or rather, the aggression against the BH republic, the armed forces of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia-Herzegovina were represented by the Territorial Defence. This is what the situation was like on paper. But at the time the Territorial Defence had been significantly weakened, because the staff members of the Territorial Defence had been significantly reduced. The number of staff members had been reduced, and the Territorial Defence had been left by members of certain ethnic groups. For example, many Serbs left the Territorial Defence, and some Croats also left the Territorial Defence, but not as many.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since Bosnia and Herzegovina was -- since Bosnia and Herzegovina obtained independence but didn't have armed forces, could you tell me what sort of decisions were made to organise the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was responsible for the defence of the country, and they issued decree laws. The first decree law was one on an imminent threat of war; then there was a decree law on renaming the republican staff of the Territorial Defence and calling it the staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and then there were a number of documents that were very important as far as creating an armed defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you have a look at document 1650, 1651, and 1649, and tell me whether these documents reflect what you have just been telling us about. Could you please find out who -- could you tell us who issued document 1650. What does this document state? And on page 4, could you read out the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: 1650, on the last page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I apologise for the interruption, but again, simply for the for the record, we note that these three documents - 1650, 1651, and 1649 - do not at this time have English language translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The transcript will reflect the fact that we don't have the translations of these documents. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as far as document 1650 is concerned, who drafted the document, what is it about, and could you please read out on page 4 the decision? It's in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: These minutes from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's from the 65th session of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was held on the 4th, 5th, 6th of April, 1992. The text says: "The Presidency, at its session, in accordance with amendment 51 and 73 to the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, took the following decisions, or rather, issued the following decree laws: On declaring an imminent state of war; on changing the name of Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; on dismantling the republican staff of Territorial Defence and on creating a staff of Territorial Defence for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And the signature is the signature of the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, on page 5, could you read out the third paragraph from below.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: You mean "the presidency."?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, "the presidency."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: "The presidency appointed as commander of the territorial staff -- defence staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Hasan Efendic, and Colonel Stipan Siber was appointed as the chief of staff of the Territorial Defence in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." It's signed by the president of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, the following decision, the number is 1651, can you please tell me what the title of the decision is, and can you please tell me what the decision is all about, if you know.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The title is "Decision on Uniting all Armed Forces in the Territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It's signed by the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. I've looked at this and I can see that all the armed forces in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which existed at the time were supposed to be united.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you now please look at the document number 1649. Can you please tell me what this document represents, who was it issued about, who was it forwarded to, and the title of this decision.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 1649. This should be the next decision.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I apologise, I have skipped a few documents. This document is a decision on the recognition of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state. It is signed by the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman. And this document means that the Republic of Croatia recognised the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, can you please tell me, to what extent did the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina try to establish the way the war and the fighting would be conducted? Did they also issue an enactment which would represent the strategy of the armed fight?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I know that the Presidency did issue us the so-called platform for the armed fight, and from the military point of view, this is the strategy of defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document 0392. This document has a translation. As a soldier, would you be able to tell us what this document is supposed to refer to, and who issued it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Please give me a moment to find my bearings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document is the first -- the fourth from the beginning of the binder.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: You said 0392.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I've found it. This is the staff of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The date is 12 April 1992. And this is an instruction for the defence of the sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, signed by Commander Colonel Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In military terms, after a decision on the strategy of the fight has been issued, was the military duty-bound to issue documents to define the strategy, such as this one?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. Once the platform is issued by the Presidency, directives issued by the commander of the Territorial Defence followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did there come a time in 1992 when the city of Sarajevo and the Presidency, as the command, were cut off from the rest of the country? What problems were created in terms of the further organisation of defence?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At the beginning of May 1992, the city of Sarajevo, as the capital of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was completely blocked. This is where the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was, as well as the command of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This caused major problems outside the town of Sarajevo because it was impossible to communicate with the city of Sarajevo. There were major military -- problems for the military, because the regional and municipal staffs could not establish adequate communication with their superior command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in the territory of Zenica at the time, the district of Zenica, can you tell us what was going on in the territories outside of Sarajevo? How were units of the Territorial Defence established and organised?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I was in the territory of Zenica at the time. After the documents that we have just discussed were issued, we embarked on the organisation of the Territorial Defence in the region of Zenica. At that time, I've already said, there were plans on paper for the organisation of the Territorial Defence; however, in practice, the Territorial Defence was not organised at the beginning of the war. The Territorial Defence was supposed to be organised in order to put up a defence against the aggression, the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What forms of organisation did the Territorial Defence take at the time? What units did the Territorial Defence have at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In the territory of Zenica, the main command body was the regional staff of Territorial Defence. It had its subordinate units in various municipalities. Those were municipal staffs of the Territorial Defence. And within the framework of the municipal staffs, there were units of Territorial Defence. Again, I'm saying this was only on paper, this was pursuant to plans; however, in reality, this was very complex and it was very different, and I told you why there were no units as such at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army, as you've already told us, had its reserve at the time and it turned into a force attacking Bosnia-Herzegovina, how were militarily able-bodied men organised? Did they all join the Territorial Defence, or did something else happen in the field?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Things were completely different in the field, because units of Territorial Defence could not be established straight away. In April there were a number of refugees arriving in the region of Zenica. The situation was rather chaotic. We had a number of volunteers who organised themselves into the units of patriotically inclined citizens who wanted to defend the republic of Bosnia and Hercegovina from aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people who were rallied around the so-called patriotic forces who wanted to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, to what extent did they accept the command of the municipal staffs and the regional staff of the Territorial Defence? Were they those that decided to act did quite independently?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: After the decision that I've already referred to, most of the patriotic forces which had organised themselves placed themselves under a joint command. Some of those patriotic forces that had organised themselves and which were under the influence of various power-wielders, private individuals, influential people in towns and in villages, did not place themselves immediately under the command of the Territorial Defence. With time, those independent patriotic forces or units of people who wanted to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina organised themselves in different places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, what tools, what facilities and armaments did the Territorial Defence have at its disposal in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I can only speak about the area that I performed my duties. I know that the arms of the Territorial Defence was under the control of the JNA, because it had been placed in the barracks of the JNA or in the depots of the JNA. I've already told you that all those weapons had been taken away from the Territorial Defence, and it cannot be accessed. In the barracks where those weapons could be found, I know of a number of cases in the territory where I worked that these depots had been blown up Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by the JNA and the weapons of the Territorial Defence was thus completely destroyed. In the entire region, I had only one case of some of the weapons having been given to one brigade. Those weapons were mostly infantry weapons, without artillery, without shells, without grenades. In other words, some weapons were given to this brigade, but it couldn't be used in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, at that time, what were the detachments and units of the Territorial Defence armed with? What kind of weapons were those? And to what extent did people employ their own private means in order to obtain weapons?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In such a situation that I've just described as being really chaotic, in light of the fact that the Territorial Defence did not have any weapons, people resorted to the black market where they obtained weapons. They joined the so-called patriotic groups that I've just mentioned. They're names were varied. I know that there were the so-called Patriotic League, that there was the Green Berets, that there were different legions; there was a force called MOS, and so on and so forth. Anyway, people obtained weapons for their own money, and again this was infantry weapons. There were very few automatic rifles, militarily, whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me, what facilities did the Territorial Defence have at its disposal, and what staff, what personnel, did the Territorial Defence have at its disposal that enabled them to organise themselves in such a complex situation?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: One should point out that all Bosniak patriots joined the Territorial Defence, those who wanted to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were also the Serbian people; there were also some Croats. But mostly they were Bosniaks. Why was that? Some of the Serbs joined the Yugoslav People's Army; others volunteered or were reservists, or they joined the army of Republika Srpska. I must say that the staff that was left was not skilled, was not professional, and their education was minimal. We did not have any barracks, any facilities. We mostly used premises of various companies or private houses where we billeted commands of particular detachments and companies that were being formed and replenished at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the commander of the regional staff of the Territorial Defence, who were you superior to?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: As the commander of the staff, I was superior to the municipal staffs of the 12 municipalities that formed the region of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, who was your superior -- which was your superior command?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At the time, my superior command was the staff of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have described the conditions that prevailed when the Territorial Defence was being created. You have described the means that you had at your disposal. Can you please tell me very briefly, what were the military circumstances that prevailed in the territory of the regional staff of Zenica? What was the military situation? Did you face any combat operations in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The military situation was very complex. The aggressor had a major advantage at the beginning of the war. They expelled a lot of the population that mostly moved into the territory where I was commander. In practical terms, some of the municipalities had been occupied. It was very difficult at the time to put any -- put up any defence and stop the aggressor's advancement. We did not have any weapons; we did not have enough weapons to resist -- to put up any resistance against the aggressor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your major combat tasks at the time, in what areas, and what were the military results of those operations?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At that time we endeavoured to stop the aggressor, if nothing else. We were successful to a certain extent. If I'm looking at the left and the right flanks of the area where I was commander, the complete municipality of Kupres had been occupied; part of Bugojno had already been occupied; Donji Vakuf was completely occupied; part of Travnik had been occupied; and especially the Vlasic plateau had been taken; part of territory of Novi Travnik had also been occupied. The aggressor had reached the borders and took the most prominent facilities above the town of Zenica. It had already Zepce and Zavidovici municipalities in their hands as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you told us that the capital and the main command in Sarajevo were completely blocked off and cut off from the rest of the country. To which extent could you receive any of the decisions of the Main Staff? To which extent were their decisions a reflection of what was going on in the field?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I said that it was very difficult to communicate with the superior command. I said that it was difficult to forward written documents to subordinate commands. And members of the Territorial Defence staff did not have an accurate vision of the situation in the field, because the units, the subordinate units, weren't able to provide reports on what was happening in the surroundings. When the communications with the superior command were cut off, I know that we had two very modest forms of communications: We had radio contact that we used, the equipment was very poor; and the second link we managed to use was sort of a link used within the railway system. It was very susceptible to breaking down. So as a commander I wasn't able to receive these decisions taken at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you have a look at the documents under B, DH212-0431, 0432, 0441, 0454, 0455, 0456, 0465, 467, 468, 472, 473, DH216-0481, 482, 483, and 484. And could you have a brief look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, after the break, I only have a few questions that I would like to ask the general about all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness will have enough time to examine the documents during the half-an-hour break. We will resume at about 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume after our technical break. Defence counsel may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I think you've had the opportunity of having a look at these documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of one document, could you tell me whether the other ones are from the Main Staff of the armed forces, or rather, the Supreme Command staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether, in 1992, this command was your superior command, or is it some other military body?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, in the documents that I've examined, the body concerned was my superior body, that is to say, it was my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In some of the documents, reference is made to the Main Staff of the armed forces, whereas the other documents mention the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces. Is the command concerned the same one, is it the same superior command, and if that is the case, could you tell me whether at that time the names in the BH army were frequently changed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, the command is the same one. It's just the name that has changed. And obviously, in the course of the war, there were frequent changes within the structure and as far as the names of commands and units are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably noticed that some of these orders relate to the area where you were the commander of the regional staff. You have already said that at the time communication was difficult between Sarajevo and your superior command. Could you tell me whether at that time you received all these decisions, or rather, all these orders from your superior command?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I have already told you quite precisely what sort of problems we had as far as communications are concerned, as far as sending documents are concerned. I mentioned the form of communications we had. And some of these orders were not orders that I received from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the fourth document towards the end, I think it's DH216, but I'll tell you the exact number in a minute. It's DH216. Can you see the document? It's document number 15. It's from the Supreme Command Staff, and it's a document being forwarded to the commands of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. I have found that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a document on the formation of the corps of the BH army. It's dated the 18th of August, 1992. Does this document confirm what you have just said; namely, that some decisions did not arrive in good time, and as a result it was necessary for them to be forwarded again to subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, this document quite obviously demonstrates that that is the case. It was necessary to forward the relevant document to the subordinate unit again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the fourth document in the series of these documents. It's numbered DH212.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness mentioned the 18th of August, 1992. DH216 is dated the 11th of October, 1992. So I wanted to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you have a look at the second page of the document, at the bottom it says: "When the decision on creating a corps was taken," it's that date that the witness was referring to. And it was necessary to forward it again on the 11th of October, 1992, because at the time the decision was taken, it wasn't possible to forward it to subordinate units. I think that that is the date that the witness was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, the document dated the 18th of -- is dated the 18th of October, 1992, but it was forwarded on the 11th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could we now have a look at the first document in this section. The first one, the number is DH212, what sort of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This is a document from the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's a decision on forming units of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's signed by the Chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces, Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in which area should these units and brigades listed under 1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13, in which areas should these units and brigades have been formed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This decision stated that these units that you have mentioned here should be formed in the territory that was in the zone of responsibility of the regional defence staff in Zenica, and I was at the head of this staff at the time. So of these -- out of these brigades, I was not able to form these units, I was only able to form the 1st Zenica Brigade. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The only document that we have mentioned and that you -- the number is 0472. This is a document that doesn't come from the Supreme Command Staff. Could you tell me who drafted this document? 0472 is the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found the document. This document is from the War Presidency of Banja Luka municipality. It's forwarded to the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was forwarded from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look at paragraph 4, what is being requested in this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: They're requesting that the 1st Banja Luka Brigade be formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the following document: 0473.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Stop, please. [Interpretation] Just a minute, there's a problem with the transcript. Defence counsel, please continue. No, it's not working. Apparently it's working now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you to have a look at the following document: 0473 [Realtime transcript read in error "0173"]. Could you tell me what it states? Did the Supreme Command Staff accept the decision made by the Banja Luka War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The Supreme Command Staff accepted the suggestion that was made by the Banja Luka Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My following question was whether you, as the commander of the regional staff, were aware of the fact that, in 1992, this Banja Luka Brigade was formed; and did it become part of the Banja Luka -- I'm sorry, of the Zenica regional staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: While I was the commander of the regional staff, this unit was not formed in the area of the Zenica regional staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 22, there's a mistake. The number is wrong. The number should be - I apologise - 473 and not 173. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In addition to the fact that you were defence and stopping the JNA forces and the Serbian forces in the peripheral areas that you have mentioned, tell me whether at any point in time were you assigned tasks, and were you ordered to engage in other combat action? And if so, what sort of combat action was ordered, and what forces was used?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In addition to my main task, which was to defend the territory -- that was my main task, I was to defend the territory from the aggression. In addition to that task, in the zone of responsibility that I had, I received from the Supreme Command Staff the task of singling out forces for lifting the blockade of Sarajevo. To the extent that it was possible to do this, I should find forces to lift the blockade of the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent was the issue of lifting the blockade of Sarajevo one of the main military and strategic issues that you were faced with in 1992, and, in fact, throughout the entire war?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, as a soldier, it was quite clear to me that if the aggressor took Sarajevo, which was the capital of -- which is the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in such a case, he would have realised his objectives and Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been completely occupied. I believed the task I had been given to be a very important one, and if I had available forces, I used them to try and lift the blockade of Sarajevo. There were numerous men who volunteered to join the action to lift the blockade of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say there were a lot of volunteers, could you tell us whether these men were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or were they from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: They were citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I organised all those I could to form units. I knew there were men who volunteered to fight in the territory to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. They were citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, at any point in 1992, did a group from the Supreme Command Staff come from Sarajevo, and did they have the same task? Were they to mobilise all the available forces in order to try, once again -- in order to try to lift the blockade of Sarajevo once again, in order to make a new attempt?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: We tried to lift the blockade even before that on several occasions; however, we were not successful. From the Main Staff, a delegation came to my office, headed by Mr. -- General Hadzihasanovic. He showed us a document from the Main Staff and explained to us what the goal of this document was. As far as I could understand at the time, I saw that General Hadzihasanovic's goal was to organise units in the territory of the regional staff of Zenica, and to prepare them to embark on lifting the blockade from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have explained to us the situation that prevailed in the territory of the regional staff of Zenica. The arrival of the group in that area, did it make you think that the Main Staff did not have at their disposal the accurate information on the situation on the ground? And did you have at the time all the nine brigades that were envisaged by the documents that you saw a little while ago, under number DH212?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At that time I was convinced that the staff of the Supreme Command did not have the accurate information about the situation on the ground, especially in my territory, in the territory under my command. And I realised that this group was there only to unite the units and to channel them towards lifting the blockade from Sarajevo. The group that had arrived from the Main Staff, I believe that they had similar information; however, when they visited us, they realised that there were no such units in place that would be capable of lifting the blockade there and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, are you aware of what information did the working group provide to the Main Staff? And after that, was the mission of that task force, or the working group, changed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic was the leader of that task force. After I provided him with detailed information, to the extent that he, as a military expert, was able to gain an insight into the situation, he tried to organise units. However, I told him what the problems were, and after that he realised that in the period of time that he envisaged, he could not implement the mission that he was given by the Main Staff. And I know that General Hadzihasanovic informed the Main Staff of the armed forces of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was General Hadzihasanovic's mission? What mission was he given after he provided the Main Staff with the accurate information?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic realised what the situation was; he fully appreciated the situation. And I have to emphasise here that at that time, in the territory of the regional staff of defence, there were even bigger problems, because the aggressor had been successful in the territory of the municipality of Jajce, so the situation was even more chaotic than before. And General Hadzihasanovic realised that I had not been able to establish the corps pursuant to my orders, because during that period of time, I did not have enough troops, I didn't have enough men to form the 3rd Corps. And I know that General Hadzihasanovic sent a proposal to the Main Staff in order to help the establishment of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the territory of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the decision of the Main Staff after that? And what was the position of General Hadzihasanovic after that, and what was your position after that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The staff of the Supreme Command issued a decision to speed up the establishment of the 3rd Corps, and they appointed General Hadzihasanovic as the commander of the 3rd Corps. I myself was appointed the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What steps did you take in order to implement the decision of the Main Staff on the establishment of the corps and its units?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic and I inspected the grounds; we did it very quickly because we didn't have a lot of time at our disposal. I issued adequate orders to the municipal staffs, and General Hadzihasanovic drafted a proposal as to what the structure of the 3rd Corps could be at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of mutual relationship did you build, General, in light of the fact that you had a very high military position and in light of the fact that a person appeared who had assumed the highest position in the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I have to say two things that I deemed important for the situation: First of all, I'm a soldier, and I fully appreciated the order of the Supreme Command, and I knew that I had to act on that order. Secondly, I was delighted when I heard how General Hadzihasanovic had reacted, and I realised that he was a very good soldier, a very well-educated soldier, with very strong integrity. And I didn't mind at all having him as a supreme commander, although I used to be the supreme commander in the area before his arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not only were you the commander of the regional staff, but you hailed from Central Bosnia. Tell me, to which extent did you extend assistance to General Hadzihasanovic when it came to his mission, and how much he trusted your proposals, the proposals that you gave him as a person who was well abreast of the situation?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I've told you that for these two reasons I did my utmost to help General Hadzihasanovic and the staff that he had established. I tried to help them to establish the 3rd Corps. Since General Hadzihasanovic had received very significant information from me regarding the prevalent situation, he took all of my proposals into account. I believe that it was very important for my commander to take my proposals into account as his subordinate officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at documents under tab C, DH220-0493, 0494; DH221-0498; and then documents without translation, 1686, 1687, 1688, 1689, 1690, 1691, 1694; and a document with translation, 0504. First of all, I would kindly ask you to indicate what these documents are all about. What do the documents without translation represent, documents from number 01690? Maybe you will find it easier to know that, at the beginning of the whole binder, you have a list of documents. If you take it out, you will find it easier to recognise the documents that I have just mentioned to you. At the very beginning of this binder, there is a list of documents with the numbers that I have just read out to you. Tab C, and the documents are 1690, 1694, and before that, 1689, 1688, 1687. Start with 1686. And the documents under these numbers, can you please tell us what these documents represent. They're all signed by you.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This is a series of orders by way of which I informed my subordinates that there would be a meeting with the corps commander in their territory, and I also informed them of the objectives of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. meeting, as well as who should attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The other documents that I have just mentioned bearing your signature, are the contents the same?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, these documents, do they confirm what you have just told us, and that is that, together with the new commander, you inspected the territory covered by the regional staff in order to provide the new commander with an insight into the situation which would help him to form the new brigades of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what they confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the remainder of the documents. They mostly have translations. My question is: These documents that I've just mentioned, do they demonstrate the situation in the territory? Do they also show how the decision on the mission of General Hadzihasanovic had been changed, and what efforts -- what problems you faced in your effort to establish the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I told you that I did not manage to establish the corps because of the problems that I have clearly stated here, and it is absolutely clear that General Hadzihasanovic made an effort in order to establish the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document 0519. The date is 10 December '92.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This document is from a press conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General: You, as a soldier, do you know whether the establishment of any unit, and especially of a corps, is it an easy task?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: As a soldier, I know that the establishment of any unit is a very tall order, and the higher ranking the unit is, the more complex the task gets. When it comes to the establishment of the 3rd Corps, I know that in the times of peace, in modern armies, it would take at least five to six months to establish a corps. Some armies would take even a year to establish a corps pursuant to the order for the establishment of the corps in the territory of the municipality of Zenica. At that time, we had very little time at our disposal to establish the 3rd Corps from the units which did not exist but on paper. In reality, we did not have any units of the 3rd Corps at the time. First, units had to be established, and then we could start talking about the establishment of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At this press conference, General Hadzihasanovic, as the commander of the 3rd Corps, answered a number of questions put to him. If you look at what he was talking about, the statement on the last page, that is, on page 3 of the B/C/S version, would you agree with the statement that was given by Commander Hadzihasanovic, according to which the formation of any army is not an easy task? And that in a number of states, it takes years, and he emphasised that the given time was much too short for any exceptional organisation to be established?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I completely agree with what General Hadzihasanovic said at this press conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent is the training of the troops important, and how important is it for the establishment of any military unit?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: When it comes to the establishment of a unit, the major requirement is the professionalism of the personnel. And this is followed by a number of activities that have to be undertaken by these professionals in order to establish this unit and in order to discipline such a unit and prepare it to perform its task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the first page of this document, and look at the part talking about the training centre. In this part, General Hadzihasanovic says that the training centre will provide for the training of staff up to the level of battalion commander; the second segment is the training of sabotage units, engineers, and those; and the third part is the training of foot soldiers. Training will be carried out in Zenica and some other towns. What General Hadzihasanovic said at the beginning of the establishment of the corps, and your understanding that, from the very outset, he was aware that the training of staff and their professional education was the necessary condition for creating an army that he would be able to command.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: When we, as a team, tried to form the corps, while I should point out that the corps command, which was formed but wasn't fully staffed, it was composed of personnel who weren't professional enough, they didn't have the adequate professional level. And we couldn't even find first assistants for the corps commander who had the adequate professional level. Only two of us had completed military academy, General Hadzihasanovic and myself. All the others had partially completed the military academy, but most of the staff members in the corps hadn't completed a military school of any kind. Naturally, General Hadzihasanovic took numerous measures in order to train the personnel in the corps and to train the personnel in the brigades. The units that we did form at the level of a brigade, we weren't able to appoint brigade commanders who had completed military schools, and in some brigades, we had men who had only completed secondary school. But we proceeded in this manner in order to form the 3rd Corps, to the extent that this was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, the 7th Muslim Brigade is one of the 3rd Corps brigades. Tell me, why did you suggest to General Hadzihasanovic that a brigade should be formed and called in this way? And was this an exceptional situation in the military history of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or was this -- such a tradition already in existence?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This was not the first time that a Muslim brigade was formed within the army. As far as I know my history, at the time of the Austro-Hungarian army, there were brigades composed of Muslims, of Bosniaks, and as far as I know, they fought exceptionally well. Such Muslim brigades composed of Bosniaks were also formed in the Second World War when fighting against fascism. And I know that such brigades were exceptionally successful. It wasn't a problem to form one such brigade in the 3rd Corps, since the situation was particularly complex. The situation when this brigade was formed was exceptionally complex. Since I was often present in the field, we noticed that after the fall of Jajce, when the aggressor had taken Jajce, he had taken part of the territory of Travnik, and especially the area called Karaula. We had a lot of men there who were not organised and who had come from the area of Krajina, from Jajce municipality. And they wanted to organise themselves and form a brigade that would be called the Muslim Brigade. This is what I observed in the field, and as a result, I suggested that such a brigade be formed, the brigade formed of Muslims, that is to say, of Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
