utterances.text: General, at the time in the BH army, did all its members, regardless of the ethnic group or religion they belonged to, for all these people, were there rules which allowed them to express themselves freely and practice their religion, which was not the case in the JNA, where people couldn't practice their religion when serving in the army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I must say that units in the Territorial Defence, or in the regional Territorial Defence staff, or rather, in the area where I was commander, were composed of members of all the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The men were mixed, of mixed ethnic composition. And I also suggested that a brigade be formed which would consist mainly of Muslims. And religion was allowed in all units. All religions were tolerated in all units. This was not the case in the JNA where I served and where one was not free to practice one's religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You embarked on forming the corps command and the corps in the conditions that prevailed at the time. Tell me, could you describe the structure of the corps for us. You were all professional soldiers. What sort of a structure did you plan, on the basis of what sort of establishment? And to what extent was it possible to realise your objectives?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: A corps command and corps units were supposed to be formed in accordance with establishment rules. I remember that within a corps, there was a mechanised brigade, there were motorised brigades, and there were mountain brigades. When we started forming those brigades, we realised we didn't have sufficient equipment, we didn't have men with the adequate professional level. So we weren't able to fully form those brigades, we were only able to form them to a certain extent. So we weren't able to form brigades in accordance with the establishment rules. We weren't even able to form the corps command in accordance with the establishment rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you issued an order stating how the brigades should be formed, and you have just told us that you weren't successful in doing this. But could you tell us whether issuing an order also means that a certain military unit will be formed, or rather, to what extent is this a process? And when you compare the time in which the order was issued, well, what sort of results did you obtain towards the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: As I said, forming such units, especially units of such a high level, is especially difficult. We, as professionals, tried to form both a corps command and corps units in accordance with the orders we had been issued. We wrote all this down on paper. It was very nice to see such documents, but we weren't able to put this into practice, we weren't able to implement the orders. The fact that an order has been drafted doesn't mean that the order has been successfully carried out. I'll just provide you with one example. When we formed the 1st Mechanised Brigade, we should have had about a hundred tanks in order to form this brigade, but we only had a few tanks at the time. So we couldn't even have formed one tank platoon, let alone a brigade. We needed quite a lot of time to form the corps, but we saw that we were partially successful. From the beginning, when we started forming the corps, and up until the end of 1993, we noticed that we had been successful to a certain extent. But this is far from what the corps should have looked like if it was to function according to the criteria that applied in all the armies throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, earlier on you mentioned the personnel. When a state of war is declared, naturally, according to our laws, general mobilisation was proclaimed. Given the equipment that you had, were you able to take in all the men who were to be mobilised, or rather, what percentage of the men mobilised had arms at the time in the units of your corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I have mentioned the problems that we encountered back in 1992 when we formed Territorial Defence units. It wasn't possible for us to supply 3rd Corps units with equipment and arms. It's well known that there was a ban on arming the BH army, and the units which were part of the 3rd Corps had inadequate equipment, inadequate weapons, insufficient weapons. And according to our assessments, not even 20 per cent of the men in the 3rd Corps units were armed, so not even a minimum had been satisfied in order to carry out the basic tasks of a modern corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the personnel and the structure of the command of the corps and the commands of the brigades. But tell me, how important is it to have trained commanders of platoons and companies? And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what was the situation in the 3rd Corps like at that level?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, whenever a soldier took stock of his unit, well, he believed it was important for his officers to be well trained. These are commanders of detachments, of platoons, of companies, and higher level commanders that at the time, when appointing these men as platoon and company commanders and commanders of higher levels, at that time we appointed other people, too, because we did not have men who were professional enough and were able to lead these men in accordance with contemporary standards. That's why we tried to train those men very rapidly. We organised various training centres for these men, for detachment commanders and commanders at higher levels. And we also organised specialist training for certain fields within the units of the corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, what happened with the regional defence staff and with the municipal defence staffs? When BH army units were formed and they were trying to become a modern army, when this was occurring, did the role of the military formations I have mentioned change?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: When the 3rd Corps was formed, it was suggested that the regional defence staff, the regional Territorial Defence staff, be disbanded in the Zenica area. And the regional staff continued to function for a very short period of time. It was a halfway situation. The Regional Staffs continued to function until mid-1993, I think, and that is when the municipal staffs were also disbanded. General Enver Hadzihasanovic, in my opinion, found a good solution. In the corps command, he formed a department for unifying the work of municipal staffs. We called this detachment for municipal structures, because the municipal staffs were still responsible for areas where they were formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were the commander of the regional Territorial Defence staff, and then you became the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. Who took over your duties, or rather, before the regional staffs were disbanded, did you hold only one position or did you hold two positions?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Since we knew that the regional staffs of the Territorial Defence were going to be disbanded, naturally we thought that it wasn't necessary to appoint someone else as commander. So we appointed an acting commander, and I then practically -- in practical terms, became the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. So this was a transitory period and we decided it wasn't necessary to appoint new commanders, we just appointed an acting commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what sort of staff did -- the municipal Territorial Defence staff, you said that these were area-based units.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The municipal staffs then had an -- had anti-sabotage detachments. The name itself is very significant. But these were people who were quite old. They weren't adequately armed; on the whole they had infantry weapons, hunting weapons; there were not many automatic weapons. These were not manoeuvre units; they couldn't carry out manoeuvre tasks. They were based in a given area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the problems you had as far as command staff is concerned and as far as weapons are concerned. Tell me, in 1993, how was control and command functioning from the level of the 3rd Corps command down to the level of an ordinary soldier? And what sort of problems did you encounter? As the case in all armies, was it normal for a soldier to carry out an order once a commander had issued an order?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, this is a very complex problem, and these are problems that you find in the most modern and the best-equipped army and in corps. And this was particularly the case in the 3rd Corps. We issued orders, according to which certain tasks were to be carried out. We received reports from subordinate units, reports on the implementation of these tasks. But the normal process that is followed in units throughout the world, this process involves controlling how orders were carried out. Representatives of the corps command were sent to subordinate units to control the extent to which orders were carried out. Naturally, in such situations, if communications are not adequate and if our links are not adequate, then it's possible for an order issued by the 3rd Corps command not to reach each soldier at all times and in all areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell me, to what extent did you and General Hadzihasanovic and all the members of the command often find that it was necessary to explain, persuade, and relay certain orders -- to what extent was it necessary to persuade your own commanders and soldiers to carry out these orders in order to establish command and control?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult in the case of a soldier in a modern army, but in the 3rd Corps, it was even more difficult to carry this out. We issued orders. We went into the field to control the situation. We received reports from the field, but these reports did not sometimes accurately reflect the situation in the field. We sometimes had to draft additional orders to ensure that the first order we had forwarded was carried out. So sometimes orders from the corps command wouldn't even reach the first subordinate unit. In certain cases, we couldn't forward an order to the first subordinate unit. But it's necessary for the soldiers in these units to be immediately informed of these orders, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at the other tabs. Skip tab C and look at the documents which are listed after tab D. The documents are DH158, number 1; DH158, number 2; DH158, number 3; DH158, number 4; DH0613; 1728; then DH154, document 5; 1738; 0715; 0724; 0758; DH0773; DH154, document 7; 0805; DH1454, document 8; DH1454, document 9; 1771; DH0880; DH0896; 0917; DH154, document 10; DH158, document 5; 0996; DH156, document ID [as interpreted]; DH158, document 7; document 1038; DH158, document 8; DH154, document 11; 1183; 1215; 1296; 1300; 1298; 1312; DH154, document 12; DH128; DH158, document 10. Please look at these documents, briefly. In reference to these documents, can you please tell me, do these documents reflect some of the efforts that you invested during the period while the corps was being established in order to establish it, train people, organise its structure according to the plan, discipline the army, and so on and so forth? Can you please look at all these documents and, firstly, tell me whether you recognise them as documents issued by the 3rd Corps, and then answer the questions that I've just put to you.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise them as documents issued by the 3rd Corps. This is probably just one set of documents issued by the 3rd Corps in order to establish the 3rd Corps according to its formation. The corps command, in addition to the task that it had in terms of training, in such a sort period of time - and I've already spoken quite a lot about that - the 3rd Corps command also did quite a lot in order to discipline its troops. That's why certain organisational units were established within the corps and within the corps units. We informed our subordinate units and the troops about the orders and international documents that any army should adhere to. We requested from our subordinate units to educate troops, to discipline soldiers, to take a number of measures which would serve to discipline and train the troops in accordance with rules and regulations. However, having said that, we had a number of problems that we faced at the time, not even to mention the problems in our environment. We tried to establish cooperation with the civilian structures; we also established cooperation with the civilian police. All this in our effort to educate and train, as well as discipline, our corps units and the corps itself the way they should have been organised, the way we wanted them to be organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to disciplining the troops, did the corps establish the necessary bodies, such as the military police? Did it request its subordinate units to establish such bodies? Were there military courts established? Was the responsibility of brigade commanders and other commanders established when it came to instituting disciplinary and other measures for those soldiers which did not obey rules and laws?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The corps command did embark on the organisation of special bodies which would be engaged in disciplining troops. In addition to training that we carried out, or at least tried to carry out at all the levels, starting from the highest to the lowest, to the lowest foot soldiers, we also established the military police within the corps; we established the military police at the level of the brigade; we also established disciplinary courts at the level of our brigades; we established the military court which was not under the command of the corps. We had a very close cooperation with all of these bodies. Our military police was not equipped or trained well enough. Very often when the military police implemented their tasks, we had to ask the civilian police to assist us. Brigade commands took a number of disciplinary measures, starting from various reprimands, taking troops into custody. A lot of actions were undertaken in order to discover perpetrators of various crimes. We filed complaints and instituted proceedings with the military prosecutor's office and the military court. Everything that the corps command was able to do they did in order to discipline soldiers and officers who were members of the 3rd Corps and its units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell me, what were the conditions like when you did all that? Was the situation peaceful or was your combat situation rather complex at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: It would have been ideal if we had had conditions to carry out all of these activities; however, it is very difficult to comprehend the situation that the 3rd Corps was in. From the moment the 3rd Corps was established, the situation in the territory under the control of the 3rd Corps was getting more complex by the day. I've already said what the situation was at the beginning, when the 3rd Corps was first established. At that time we had only one enemy, one aggressor. However, in the fourth common period, when we strived to establish the corps, the second front line was opening facing the Croatian Defence Council, and in that period of time, from January 1993 onward, we had problems with the Croatian Defence Council. Again, we had a huge wave of refugees coming to the area. There was a number of other activities which made the work and the training of the units of the 3rd Corps very complex. You can imagine the situation that it was in if I tell you that, in addition to fighting two enemies, we also had to discipline our units which were composed of the people who had lost their dearest, who had been expelled from their homes, and who had been temporarily accommodated in the territories of the municipalities that were under the command of the 3rd Corps. This was a very complex situation, extremely complex situation. The corps command, headed by General Hadzihasanovic, did not sleep for nights. For days we did not have time to eat due to all of the obligations that we had. This was a situation that is very described -- is very difficult to describe in a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever you have just told us now, General, clearly tell us that you were in a war, day in, day out. As the command of the 3rd Corps, and especially its commander, to what -- how much attention was paid to teach troops to respect international conventions? What were the measures that you took in that respect?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I know that General Hadzihasanovic did almost the impossible in order to establish, train, and discipline the 3rd Corps. Obviously we all helped him as much as we could, as much as we were able to do that, as much as our education enabled us to do that. However, when it came to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. international conventions and the international humanitarian law, we did issue orders for the soldiers to respect the international humanitarian law. Whenever we learned that those conventions were being violated, we immediately took measures. And we even conducted criminal proceedings against perpetrators. We filed reports with the military prosecutor's office, instructing them to punish such troops. We were involved in the education of our staff, and we not only issued orders, but we also explained to them the meaning of the violation of the international humanitarian law. We told them that nobody had the right to violate those conventions. And we tried as hard as we could; however, this was not easy to implement in the field, under the conditions that I have described to you. We had a number of problems that we faced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, on page 53, line 9, can the correction be made: The number of documents is DH156, which is not "ID," but a document which has already been admitted into evidence under DH156, without ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to be economical with our time, I would kindly ask you to look at all the documents after tab F. I'm going to give you five or six minutes. For the transcript, I'm going to mention all these numbers. These are DH0704; DH263; 0760; DH158, document 4; DH161, document 1; DH160, document 1; DH163, document 1; DH162, document 1; DH161, document 2; DH111, document 3; DH264; DH265; DH161, document 4; DH266; DH163, document 2; DH161, document 5; DH267; DH161, document 6; DH161, document 7; DH161, document 8; DH161, document 10; DH257; DH -- document 11; DH161, document 12; DH161, document 13; DH161, document 14; DH161, document 15; DH161, document 16; DH161, document 17; DH163, document 12; DH68; DH161, document 18; DH161, document 19; DH163, document 14; DH159, document 5; DH155, document 3; DH160, document 8; DH119; DH56; DH275; DH155, document 2; and finally, DH120. Can you please look at these documents, and I'm going to put a few questions to you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be best for the witness to have a look at the documents during the break, and you could then put the questions to the witness after the break. It's 25 to 6.00. We'll resume at about 6.00, and that will leave us with one more hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Defence again. But if the Defence refers to a document, I'd be grateful if the Defence could specify exactly which document the witness's answer refers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, having examined these documents, naturally, with the exception of documents that come from the military prosecutor's office and courts, DH119 and the others that follow, in these documents, did you recognise documents that come from the 3rd Corps of which you were the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. These documents were drafted by the 3rd Corps command and its bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in some of these documents, were you able to recognise your own signature, and could you tell me in what sort of conditions would you sign on behalf of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In the documents that I have been shown, I was able to recognise my own signature, and I was able to recognise documents that I signed on behalf of the commander. I did this when the commander was not able to sign a document and it was urgent to carry out a given task or order. In other circumstances, it was the corps commander who would sign the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This entire series of documents consists, on the whole, of orders you issued to subordinate units, or rather, they are documents that were forwarded in cooperation with other bodies to those bodies. Tell me whether you, in the 3rd Corps, only issued orders, or did you take other measures in order to ensure that your orders were actually being carried out?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: When issuing orders and implementing orders, the element of control is of crucial importance; I have mentioned this already. This is the case in all armies throughout the world. In addition, I said that there was such control on the level of the corps command, and bodies of the corps command would carry out such controls in the field. In addition, we asked for other reports if we weren't quite clear about the extent to which orders had been carried out. This was especially the case when we received information from other sources, according to which our orders were not being implemented in the field by certain soldiers. In such cases, we took additional measures, issued additional orders, and asked for further clarification from units. We asked for them to provide us with reports on what was happening in the field. These are measures that we took in addition to issuing the orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, at the time that General Hadzihasanovic was the commander, tell me, what sort of relations did you have with the civilian authorities, or rather, at any point in time did you become superior to those authorities and did you establish a military administration?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, that is to say, the 3rd Corps command, had a full understanding of its role in the defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in territory where 3rd Corps units were deployed, as well as its command. In that territory, the civilian bodies of power functioned, and they were separate from military bodies of power. That was a vast area, and the civilian authorities functioned to the extent that it was possible to function under such conditions. The corps command made attempts to cooperate with the civilian authorities, and it never placed itself above the civilian authorities, and in particular, it never tried to establish command and control over the civilian authorities. We had problems, for example, in the command in the case of mobilisation. That was the responsibility of the civilian authorities. And as far as logistics and providing food is concerned, we had problems. This was also the responsibility of the civilian authorities. Whenever we encountered problems, we requested that the civilian authorities assist us. We did speak to each other, but we never placed ourselves above the civilian authorities. We never assumed authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, on the basis of orders, and in practice, what sort of attitude did you have towards the civilian population, or rather, to what extent did your orders reflect the responsibility that each soldier had, or rather, to what extent did they reflect the sort of responsibility incurred by a soldier who would treat civilians and their property contrary to the orders?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: We couldn't issue orders to civilians and to citizens, but we could issue orders to our soldiers who were members of our bodies. We issued them orders. We tried to prevent violations of discipline perpetrated against citizens. We tried to prevent theft committed by our soldiers. There were such incidents, I can't deny that. Our soldiers did commit theft, but whenever we found out about such cases, we, within the system of command and control, took the necessary measures. A number of disciplinary activities were implemented, carried out. Naturally, we couldn't prevent each and every soldier from stealing something from the civilian population. As I have said, some of our soldiers lost everything they had in the war. They lost their family members, and it was necessary to understand that situation. Nevertheless, we would take disciplinary measures against such soldiers. And if we suspected that a crime had been committed, we would suggest that the district military courts institute criminal proceedings against such individuals and punish them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, since we are now discussing the documents under section F, from 1 to 27, could we now have a look at document DH161, document 2. This is an order dated the 18th of April, 1994. Have you found the document, DH161, document 2? It's number 5 on this list of documents.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I've found document number 1. Yes, I've found it. 162.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 161, document 2. It's under number 5. You should go two, three documents back.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 161, document 2. This is an order dated the 18th of April, 1994. It's under number 9. It's the ninth document in the list.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I can find document 1 but not document number 2. Is it -- does it follow on?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's a document that follows the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: You'll have to help me. It's an order. I found document number 1. 161, document 1, I've found that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's the eighth document from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In future, if you have such binders, it would be good to do what you did before, to have little tabs, and this will enable us to find the tab immediately. I know that takes up a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found the document, document 161, document 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in response to my previous question, you said that your orders were issued for your soldiers in cases when you could take certain measures against them. Have a look at paragraph 2 in this order. Does this paragraph, in fact, reflect what you have just said? Does it reflect that it is your responsibility to take action in the case of your own soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we'll follow your suggestion. We'll do that tomorrow. But we weren't able to do that today because there were a lot of documents, and we weren't able to organise them all. It will make it easier for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell me, what was your attitude toward the protection of religious buildings and the clergy and cemeteries?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The corps command and General Hadzihasanovic and I, as the deputy, always requested that religious buildings be protected. We requested that they not be destroyed. We said that believers should be protected. And we would take disciplinary measures against individuals who violated these instructions, and we would also criminally punish such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, given the conditions, the wartime conditions in that area, was it necessary for you to approach this issue in a very serious manner, so to speak? Was it necessary for you to ensure that the rules were respected, as is the case in all armies? Was particular attention paid to this issue because of the situation in the area, as far as the religious buildings of other peoples are concerned?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, since the corps command and its commander were in favour of religious freedom and allowed believers, regardless of their faith, to practice their religion, people were allowed to pray in accordance with their religious beliefs. Given this attitude, we were very concerned by religious buildings being destroyed, we were concerned by the maltreatment Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of certain religious groups, so sometimes we had to use the military police to secure such buildings, if we believed that a religious building might be damaged. We thought that this was the right of every citizen. It was every citizen's right to practice his or her religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the documents I have shown to you, did you come across any such orders, orders in which the corps commander requested a particular form of protection for religious buildings and for members of the clergy?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I've come across such a document in this series of documents, and this document shows that the military police was given the task of protecting religious buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document DH161, document 16. It's somewhere in the middle of the series of documents that I have shown to you. It's an order dated the 19th of June, 1993. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order by which prevention of arrest of civilians, looting and destruction of property is ordered. If you look at item 4, within the general protection, does this order confirm exactly what you have just told us, that particular attention was being paid to religious facilities and members of the clergy?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, number 4, item 4, in this order confirms precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document DH257. This is a few documents back from the one that we are looking at right now. The date is 14 June 1993. So if you go back, a few documents back, you will find this particular one.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The date is 14 June 1993, and the number of this document is DH257.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Can you please help me and instruct me what to look for in the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is under number 19, number 19 in this batch of documents, somewhere in the middle of your table there.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the corps commander, or the corps as such, starting from the things that you have just told us about, did they pay special attention to the significant monuments of religion and culture in Central Bosnia even before any combat activities ever took place?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. In the corps command, headed by General Hadzihasanovic, we issued orders to that effect and warnings to that effect, saying that if combat operations should take place in the area where there were religious facilities, that these facilities should be protected. And this is confirmed by this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this set of documents, let me ask you about the document which is second in this batch after tab F. Can you please explain: In light of your previous answer, when you became deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, you stopped performing any duties in the regional staff of Zenica. Tell me why the signature block of this document still contains your name as commander.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Because in this particular month, the month of February, we still had the regional staff; however, the number of staff was reduced, because some of the staff was transferred to the 3rd Corps command with a task to organise the 3rd Corps. By that time, the regional staff was still not disbanded. It was disbanded only later. And the regional staff was still in the position to issue orders to the municipal staffs which were previously under its authorities. In the wartimes, this was the way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this an order issued by you or by the person who was the acting commander, the person who, for the reasons specified by you, was not appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the person was appointed that would be the acting commander, and I don't see that anybody signed on his behalf. So it's very difficult for me to explain why my signature is not here if my name is indicated on the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for my intervention; however, I'm not quite clear, the Chamber is not quite clear about the previous answer. If you look at the document DH263, have you found DH263?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, DH263, in B/C/S, there's your name there but there's no signature. The document has not been signed. The name has been typed. In the left part of the English translation, it says that the document originates from the Zenica district defence staff, and this document was addressed to other municipal defence staffs, Bugojno, Gornji/Donji Vakuf, Travnik, and so on and so forth. And it is indicated here that Commander General Merdan, and under item 6, it says that "Municipal defence staff commanders will be responsible to me for the implementation of this order." So did you wear two hats at the time? Were you assigned to the 3rd Corps as an officer, but wasn't, at the same time, your position in the regional staff? Because in this order, the order is not on behalf of the municipality, it is sent to the municipality. In the month of February, our impression was that you were deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, but according to this document, you had other responsibilities as well. How do you account for that? How can you explain that? This document refers to civilian prisoners, and it says that it is forbidden to loot, and so on and so forth, and you make municipal staff commanders responsible to you. What is your explanation of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of my testimony, I've already said that when the command of the 3rd Corps was established, I was assigned the duty of deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. I was appointed to that position, and I performed those duties and tasks. When the 3rd Corps was established, the regional defence staff was not abolished and municipal defence staffs in municipalities were not abolished, they still existed. In order to provide for the chain of command some of the positions in the regional staff were kept, but acting commanders were appointed. We did not want to have commanders, because the regional staff would soon be disbanded. It is very difficult to conceive that such a huge organisation could just disappear overnight. Command over municipal staffs still goes via the regional staff, and the chain of command is from the corps via the regional staff to the municipal staffs. I was the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps; however, in order to issue command over the municipal staffs, which were territorial units, in order to establish this chain of command, we had to have this chain. As far as I can remember, the municipal staffs were abolished only in the month of June 1993. I've also testified that the corps command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Should we then conclude that, until the month of June, when the municipal staffs were abolished, you had two responsibilities: You were the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, but you were also the commander responsible for the municipalities, for the defence of the municipalities? Is it not true that you had two functions, two positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't have two functions or positions. The original staff, the original defence staff was abolished at the beginning of March 1993, as far as I can remember. At the level of the corps command, we established a department for cooperation with regional defence bodies, in order to still have a certain connection with the municipal staffs which were abolished in June, according to my information. In the course of the reorganisation of the army, we still didn't receive the order to abolish municipal staffs as regional defence units when the corps was being established. At the moment when the corps was being established and organised, when its units were being organised, our municipal staffs still functioned because no order was issued for them to be abolished. So for a certain period of time, we still had to have communication and connection between the corps command and the municipal defence staffs. That is why we appointed the acting commander of the regional defence staff in order to provide for this chain of command. This means I didn't have a dual role, I didn't have two positions. I was the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps from the 4th of February, 1993, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I will continue along the same line of questioning as the President of the Trial Chamber in order to clarify certain things which still maybe remain unclear after your answers. You have told us that your position in the regional defence staff was filled by an acting commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was de facto commander of the regional staff, was it the acting commander or you? Because your signature block was still there, who was de facto performing these duties?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: It was Mr. Ramiz Dugalic, who was appointed the acting commander of the regional staff until the moment it was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The second question that I would like to put to you is the following: Who is this document addressed to, the document that bears the signature block with your name but no signature? Who was this document addressed to?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This document was addressed to the municipal defence staffs, and here it says to which municipalities it was addressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell me, did the municipal defence staffs figure as military defence structures, or were they civilian bodies who --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The municipal defence staffs were military structures, they were not civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the municipal defence staffs as military structures in certain municipalities, were there also civilian bodies of power over which you, as a member of the army, did not have any authority? And if there were such bodies, what bodies were those?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In the territories of these municipalities, there were also civilian bodies, and they functioned according to the constitution, in keeping with the constitution. And the municipal defence staffs could not issue any orders to the civilian bodies of power. However, during the transition of power, the head of the municipality could propose his candidate for the commander of the municipal staff, because the parties that won in the elections could propose their candidates for commanders of municipal staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we look at the structure of the military authorities and the civilian authorities, did, at any point in time, any of the military units, be it a brigade or a corps or municipal or regional staffs, as military units, did they become incorporated into the structure of the civilian bodies, municipalities, war presidencies, of any other bodies that had their own tasks during the defence; or alternatively, were they part of the chain of command which went from the municipal staff to the command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Commanders of municipal staffs were entitled to attending sessions of municipal councils in order to inform themselves of the situation in the area; however, the control and the command and the chain of command Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. followed the military line of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in relation to this document, because we already mentioned who you were responsible for, as commanders, as far as implementing orders are concerned, and you mentioned who these orders related to. In item 1 of this order, who is the order intended for? And who is forbidden from acting contrary to this order?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This order is forwarded to all BH army units in the zone of responsibility of defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this an order issued to the soldiers who are members of the BH army? Does this order prohibit them from committing such acts, or is something else in question?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This is a prohibition issued to BH army members, because units of municipal staffs were also members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the zone of responsibility. What sort of tasks did the 3rd Corps and its units have in the zone of responsibility, or rather, what did you take the meaning of the zone of responsibility of BH army units to be?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, the definition of "zone of responsibility" is very simple, but in practice it's a very complex matter. A zone of responsibility in brigades or a zone of responsibility in a corps only involved the responsibilities of soldiers of the BH army. It didn't concern civilians, international organisations, refugees; it didn't concern those who were circulating in the zone of responsibility of the brigade or the corps. A zone of responsibility is a zone where combat action is ongoing, and the commander is responsible for his soldiers in that area. But naturally, a commander is responsible for his soldiers wherever these soldiers might be. So the zone of responsibility only concerns responsibility for soldiers who are under the authority of a particular commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to move on to another subject that I would like to examine with you. This concerns the relations of the BH army and the HVO. General, in 1992, when you were the commander of the Territorial Defence regional staff in Zenica, at that time, in addition to Territorial Defence units, were HVO units being formed in the area of your region?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: HVO units were being formed. They existed in all municipalities where the regional defence staff had its zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of relations developed between the Territorial Defence and the HVO in 1992, given that at the beginning of your testimony, you had said that, in accordance with a Presidency decision, the Territorial Defence represented the only armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in accordance with the constitution in force in the country?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In practice, we tried to talk to the units and commands of the HVO and we tried to act jointly in response to the aggression carried out by the Serbian forces. At the time I wasn't able to reach a common position with the HVO command. It wasn't possible for us to engage in defending the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The HVO was involved in other activities, although they said that they were fighting the side that had committed an aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arriving in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at the very beginning of the war, in the territory of Central Bosnia, did you encounter any different political objectives expressed by one of the parties in power, by the HDZ? And if so, could you tell me what sort of objectives they had?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I had certain information, and I was able to see a tape in which leaders of the HDZ stated that their objectives were to create a state for the Croatian people, and to ensure that the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in which the majority was Croatian, joined Croatia. They wanted to annex this part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have already heard evidence about the composition of the population in Central Bosnia, could you tell us whether such political objectives amounted to denying the existence of other peoples? The attitude of these leaders, did this pose a risk? Did that attitude pose a risk?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, it's quite clear that we had to fight for a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina, a country that had obtained international recognition. And we believed that the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be divided yet. The objectives expressed by some representatives of the HDZ showed that they wanted the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to their statements, it was necessary to annex part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia. And naturally, our positions were different, so this had to result in problems in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said, in 1992, in Central Bosnia, the HVO armed forces were being formed, could you tell us whether those forces accepted the command of the regional or Territorial Defence staff as a legitimate defence force? And did you make any attempts to unify the armed forces in the area with one common objective, that is to say, with the objective of mounting a defence against the enemy who had attacked the country?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The HVO at that period of time had units in various areas which were preventing the aggressor from penetrating in the direction of Central Bosnia. At that time we couldn't establish common objectives, although the HVO stated that they were fighting the aggressor in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But we tried to establish joint commands, we tried to act jointly in certain areas, in order to prevent the aggressor from penetrating further into Central Bosnia. I remember making a suggestion. We said that in the Lasva Valley, the commander of all units of the HVO and of the Territorial Defence should be Mr. Filip Filipovic, who is now a retired general of the federation army, just like myself. And it was suggested that I should be his deputy. But the HVO did not accept this suggestion. So I made attempts; I strove to create a joint command and to act jointly against the same aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since, as you have just said, these suggestions were not accepted, did the fact that there were two armies in the same area, and did the fact that they had various political objectives, result in armed clashes as early as 1992? And do you have any personal experience of such clashes?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, it's quite clear that two armies cannot operate in one area if there is not -- if they don't have a joint command. In spite of my efforts to create a joint command, I personally had problems as far as carrying out such a task is concerned. On a number of occasions, I was arrested by members of the HVO. This was an affront to my dignity. And I remember that at the beginning of May, I was arrested for the first time. I fared very badly. I was asked to order that the Territorial Defence units be disarmed, and to order that they be resubordinated, or rather, I was asked to request that they be subordinated to the HVO. And this is something I could not have done at that time; I did not have such authority. Naturally, when trying to resolve the difficulties that we encountered, since, in 1992, there had been a number of incidents which resulted in a number of individuals being killed. Some BH army members would be disarmed. For example, at checkpoints held by the HVO, BH army units were not allowed to pass through territory controlled by the HVO towards the Serbian aggressor, and there were a number of other incidents, from stealing from the civilian population -- there were cases of maltreatment, there were some difficult situations in which equipment was taken from the Territorial Defence, vehicles were taken from them and weapons, and Territorial Defence members were severely maltreated at the checkpoints that they passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that the first time you were arrested was in May 1992. Tell me, at the time what position did you hold in the Territorial Defence? And when you were arrested, were you physically maltreated too?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At the beginning of May, I was one of the assistant commanders of the Territorial Defence staff in Zenica. In the regional -- the commander of the regional staff in Zenica at the time was someone who is now a retired general, Ramiz Dugalic. I was then arrested by HVO units. I was physically maltreated; I was beaten. They even prepared to execute me. I felt very bad. But as a commander of the Territorial Defence, sometime in the autumn of 1992, I was arrested at a checkpoint of the HVO. They disarmed me, took me to the command, but I managed to persuade the HVO command to release me and to return my weapon to me. I was arrested as a deputy commander of the 3rd Corps too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that these were incidents, you mentioned numerous incidents that involved yourself. But tell me, in 1992, did an armed conflict break out in the territory of the regional Territorial Defence staff? And how did the Territorial Defence, or rather, army, try to deal with such situations?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Naturally, in all these cases, and in my prior testimony I have spoken about -- I spoke about this in detail, but now I would say that there were incidents which turned into armed conflicts. I will now only mention an example. For example, when the barracks in Busovaca municipality, at a place called Kaonik, were taken over, there was an incident. One Territorial Defence member was wounded and one HVO member was wounded. There was an extremely difficult situation in Gornji Vakuf, in June, and then in October. And the most difficult situation was in Novi Travnik, in October, when someone was killed in the BH army, or rather, in the Territorial Defence. In June there was a clash in Novi Travnik, but only two Territorial Defence members were killed. But in the clash in Novi Travnik in October, as far as I can remember, four to six Territorial Defence members were killed. As to the casualties that the HVO have, I had no information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we finish for the day, because, as I see, we are running out of time, tell me whether, in 1992, it's not just that a joint command wasn't established, as you said. In the territory of the regional Territorial Defence staff, did parallel civilian bodies appear? And if you have any personal information about this, could you tell us about it, briefly.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, there are two issues I would like to testify about here. One problem concerned the municipalities in the zone of responsibility of the regional Territorial Defence staff, where the population was mostly Croats; and the other problem was in municipalities where the Bosniaks were in the majority. In municipalities where the Croatian population was more numerous, the HVO established -- took power. And I saw this in an order which concerned my arrest. The HVO, at the beginning of May 1992, in the area of Busovaca, took a decision and prohibited the legal authorities from working. And all the orders from the legal authorities and the Territorial Defence staff were proclaimed to be invalid. Where the Bosniaks were in the majority, in these municipalities, parallel organs of power were established. In addition to the legal organs of power of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, HVO bodies were also established. Civilian bodies, parallel bodies were created. A parallel police force was created. They tried to use Croatian currency, and they took various other measures. They created parallel bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 7.00 p.m. We will have to adjourn now. The Defence would like to help us by placing tabs in our binders. So since we have already used the binders, I feel it might be difficult to return them to you. But I'm sure you'll do what is necessary when presenting us with new binders. General, tomorrow the hearing will start at 2.15. As I've said, you are now a witness testifying in the interests of justice, so you shouldn't have contact with anyone, you shouldn't see the Prosecution or the Defence. And we'll see you tomorrow at 2.15. I would like to thank everyone, and I will see you all at the hearing at 2.15 tomorrow.
